claims.text: The dynamic mechanical response of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes is primarily governed by a transition in the dominant deformation mechanism.
Dislocation glide dominates deformation at moderate temperatures and strain rates.
Stress-induced deformation twinning dominates at low temperatures and high strain rates.
The proposed transition from glide to twinning preserves the strength–ductility balance of FeNiCrMn.
Standard solidification produces FeNiCrMn with an equiaxed grain structure.
Standard solidification produces a typical defect density in FeNiCrMn.
Temperature and strain rate can be systematically varied in dynamic tests to capture the proposed deformation-mechanism transition.
Grain boundaries and deformation-induced twin boundaries are the structural mediators of the dynamic response.
At low temperature and high strain rate, applied stress promotes deformation twinning by overcoming a reduced thermal-activation barrier.
Deformation-induced twin boundaries act as internal barriers to dislocation motion.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate loading will produce higher yield strength than moderate-temperature, lower-strain-rate loading.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate loading will produce greater strain hardening than moderate-temperature, lower-strain-rate loading.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate loading will produce a measurable increase in twin density.
Moderate-temperature, lower-strain-rate loading will result in lower twin density and deformation dominated by dislocation motion.
Substantial annealing or extreme grain refinement may change the proposed behavior.
Failure to observe increased twinning together with unchanged yield strength and strain hardening under low-temperature, high-rate loading would falsify the proposed twinning-controlled response.
